explanation: To ABASH someone is to make them self-conscious and ill at ease, i.e. to "embarrass" them.
distractor_rationales: KEY
near-identical opening syllables; "abolish" is a sound-alike with no shared sense
"scold" is the reproof that might cause the feeling, not the feeling itself
"flatter" reverses it — flattery raises self-regard rather than deflating it
"punish" reads the social sting as a formal penalty

explanation: A rind is the natural outer covering that grows over and protects the orange; "husk is to corn" is the same natural-covering-to-thing-covered pair.
distractor_rationales: KEY
"lid is to jar" is a manufactured, detachable cover rather than one the thing grows
"bark is to forest" pairs a covering with a collection of trees rather than with the individual thing it sheathes
"pit is to cherry" is an interior part, not an outer covering
"wrapper is to parcel" is added round the thing afterwards rather than grown by it

explanation: RANCOR is long-held bitter ill will, which "spite" names most closely.
distractor_rationales: a rhyme on the same -or ending, and frankness is not ill will
another -or rhyme; "clamor" is noise, not resentment
"dread" is fear directed forward, where rancor is grievance held backward
KEY
"envy" is the adjacent bitter feeling — wanting what another has, rather than resenting a wrong

explanation: A paragraph is one of the structural divisions an essay is built from; "scene is to play" is the same division-to-whole pair.
distractor_rationales: "index is to book" is a finding aid appended to the book, not one of the divisions it is built from
"footnote is to page" is a smaller element on a larger one, but a page is not divided into footnotes
KEY
"epilogue is to novel" is an appended close rather than one of the constituent divisions
"margin is to page" is a region of the page rather than a division of the work

explanation: WHIMSICAL describes playful, imaginative caprice, which "fanciful" captures.
distractor_rationales: KEY
"wistful" is the adjacent mood of gentle longing, often confused with whimsy but quite different
"gloomy" takes the lightness out entirely
"methodical" is the opposite temper — system rather than caprice
"fleeting" borrows the changeability of whim and drops the imagination

explanation: BRUSQUE means abrupt to the point of rudeness in manner or speech, i.e. "curt".
distractor_rationales: "brisk" is the sound-alike and shares the speed while losing the rudeness
"courteous" is the manner brusqueness offends against
KEY
"hesitant" is the opposite tempo — brusqueness does not hang back
"robust" reads abruptness as vigour

explanation: A constellation is a collective noun whose members are stars; "swarm is to bees" names a collective and then its members.
distractor_rationales: a crowd is people, but an unorganised mass rather than a named, recognised grouping
KEY
"anthill is to ants" gives the dwelling rather than the group the creatures form
"herd is to pasture" pairs a collective with the place it stands in, not with its members
"flock is to migration" pairs a collective with what it does, not with what composes it

explanation: To AUGMENT is to make greater by addition, i.e. to "enlarge".
distractor_rationales: pulled in by "augur" — the two words look related and are not
"shorten" is the opposite direction of change
KEY
"borrow" adds to a store temporarily and by the wrong mechanism
"repair" restores a thing to its size rather than increasing it

explanation: To parry a blow is to turn aside an attack; "rebut is to argument" is the same turning-aside of an attack, in words rather than blows.
distractor_rationales: "endure is to insult" absorbs the attack instead of deflecting it
"hurl is to insult" delivers the attack rather than meeting it
"provoke is to quarrel" starts the hostility off
"concede is to point" yields to the attack, the reverse of parrying
KEY

explanation: TENACIOUS describes a grip that will not let go, so "dogged" is the match.
distractor_rationales: "tenuous" is the near-twin in spelling and close to the opposite in sense — thin rather than gripping
"tense" shares the first syllable and means strained, not persistent
"fickle" lets go at the first change of mind, which is the opposite of holding on
KEY
"agreeable" is the yielding a tenacious person refuses

explanation: A connoisseur is defined by discernment — take it away and the word no longer applies. "Sentinel is to vigilant" holds the same way: a sentinel who is not vigilant is not a sentinel.
distractor_rationales: novices are often eager, but eagerness is not what makes someone a novice
a common picture of a veteran rather than the thing the word requires
KEY
a recluse must be solitary; "shy" is a frequent companion trait, not the definition
discipline is typical of athletes without being what the word means

explanation: CLANDESTINE means kept hidden, especially because it would not be permitted — "secret".
distractor_rationales: clandestine dealings are often illegal, but concealment and illegality are different things
the -destine ending invites this; the two words are unrelated
secrecy is usually careful, not reckless — the association runs backwards
pulled in by the antique flavour of the word itself
KEY

explanation: A fresco is painted into wet plaster — plaster is the surface that receives it. "Etching is to copper" is the same: the copper plate is the surface the etching is cut into.
distractor_rationales: "sculpture is to marble" gives the material the work is made OUT of, not the surface it is worked onto
"tapestry is to wool" is likewise the stuff of the work rather than a surface
"mural is to gallery" gives a location instead of a medium
KEY
"watercolor is to brush" gives the tool

explanation: To ASSUAGE is to ease or lessen something painful, i.e. to "soothe" it.
distractor_rationales: a rhyme that also fits the register; persuasion changes a mind, not a pain
another -age rhyme; hurrying a trouble along is not easing it
shares the opening "ass-" and nothing else
KEY
the bare rhyme, hiding inside the word itself

explanation: VERBOSE means using more words than are needed — "wordy".
distractor_rationales: the shared verb- root; spoken rather than long-winded
a rhyme on -ose with an unrelated sense
"hollow" reads many words as empty ones; verbose speech may be perfectly substantial
pulled in by "veracious", a different word altogether
KEY

explanation: A scowl is the outward sign of displeasure and of little else; "sneer is to contempt" is a sign that is equally specific to one feeling.
distractor_rationales: pallor may follow fear, illness or shock — it does not point to one feeling the way a scowl does
a frown may mean concentration, worry or displeasure — it does not point to one feeling
"shiver is to blanket" pairs a sign with a remedy rather than with a feeling
"laughter is to comedian" gives an external cause instead of the inner state
KEY

explanation: INDIGENT means impoverished, so "needy" is the match.
distractor_rationales: "indigenous" is the near-twin word and means native-born, not poor
KEY
"indignant" is the other near-twin; outrage has nothing to do with poverty
thrift is a response to scarcity, not the condition of it
the old slander that poverty implies idleness

explanation: A metronome does not measure a tempo that already exists; it sounds a fixed reference for a player to follow. "Tuning fork is to pitch" is the same: it sounds the reference note.
distractor_rationales: KEY
an odometer records distance already travelled rather than setting a standard
a compass reports the bearing that is the case; it does not fix one
an hourglass measures time as it runs out
an anchor prevents drift instead of setting a value for it

explanation: A BULWARK is a defensive wall, and so anything that protects — a "safeguard".
distractor_rationales: the nautical company the word keeps: bulwarks are also a ship's side
KEY
"bulk" and "burden" pull the word toward weight rather than defence
the "bul-" opening read as an eruption
another nautical neighbour; a harbor shelters but is not a defence work

explanation: To be callous is precisely to be without sympathy. "Candid is to guile" works the same way: candour is the absence of guile.
distractor_rationales: a reckless person lacks caution, not danger — danger is what they disregard
vigilance consists in having attention, not in lacking it
KEY
timidity is the presence of fear
docility is the presence of obedience

explanation: To EBB is to fall away or decline, i.e. to "dwindle".
distractor_rationales: movement without the loss of quantity that ebbing carries
staying on rather than falling away
KEY
surface movement of the same water, with nothing withdrawn
dispersal in all directions rather than a steady falling away

explanation: Pruning takes away part of the shrub so that what remains is better. "Winnow is to grain" is the same operation: the chaff goes so that the grain is improved.
distractor_rationales: watering adds to the plant instead of cutting away from it
KEY
harvesting takes the crop away entire; nothing is left behind improved
fertilising is an addition, and to the soil rather than the plant
sowing puts something in at the start rather than taking part of it out

explanation: HAUGHTY describes an overbearing sense of one's own superiority — "arrogant".
distractor_rationales: the rhyme, and a child's misbehaviour rather than an adult's pride
the near-rhyme; haste is not hauteur
a pleasant temper where the word names an unpleasant one
KEY
gravity of manner read as loftiness of self-regard

explanation: A quarry is the place marble is taken out of the ground. "Well is to water" is the same: the place water is drawn up from.
distractor_rationales: a reservoir collects rainfall that arrives on its own; nothing is won out of the ground
KEY
a dairy handles milk after it has been got
a granary stores grain rather than yielding it
a kiln makes brick rather than releasing something already there

explanation: To VEX is to irritate or trouble someone, i.e. to "annoy" them.
distractor_rationales: a "vexed question" is one long under examination, which drags the sense sideways
refusal rather than irritation
letting someone off rather than troubling them
a vexed matter is often a long-delayed one; the delay is not the vexing
KEY

explanation: Hibernating is what a bear does to get through the winter. "Migrate is to goose" is the same kind of behaviour: the seasonal answer to the cold.
distractor_rationales: KEY
wolves hunt all year; nothing about it belongs to a season
moulting is periodic but is renewal of the skin, not a response to winter
a mole burrows to live, not to survive a particular season
grazing is a daily habit rather than a seasonal one

explanation: A CACOPHONY is a harsh, discordant racket, which "din" names.
distractor_rationales: KEY
the exact opposite quality of sound
the shared -phony ending, attached to sound that is organised rather than harsh
a repetition of sound, with nothing said about harshness
the noise of a dispute rather than a quality of sound

explanation: The poems in an anthology existed separately first and were gathered. "Scrapbook is to clippings" is the same act of gathering things already made.
distractor_rationales: a novel's chapters are written as parts of it; they never stood alone
movements are composed as parts of the symphony from the start
bricks are made to be built with rather than gathered after the fact
KEY
a menu lists the dishes; it is not made out of them

explanation: To PILFER is to take small things that are not yours, i.e. to "steal".
distractor_rationales: the sound-alike, one letter away and unrelated in sense
what a pilferer might do afterwards, not the taking itself
the opposite use of what has been taken
"pile" heard inside the word, pulling toward spreading rather than taking
KEY

explanation: A scaffold holds things up only while the building is going up, and comes down when it can stand alone. "Crutch is to patient" is the same temporary support, laid aside once the patient can walk.
distractor_rationales: a trellis stays with the vine for as long as the vine grows
KEY
a foundation is permanent and part of the house
a buttress remains in place holding the wall
a pedestal stays under the statue for good
